rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Samīn says the construction “those are the signs” was already discussed at the beginning of Sūrat Yūnus.
rows.anchor: قد تقدم الكلام على نحو قوله " تلك آيات " في أول يونس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Qurʾānan” may be an appositive to the pronoun in “We sent it down,” or a qualifying circumstantial accusative; on either analysis that pronoun refers to “the Book.”
rows.anchor: أن يكون بدلا من ضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “Qurʾānan” is the direct object, while the pronoun in “We sent it down” is a cognate-object pronoun.
rows.anchor: مفعولا به والضمير في

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “ʿArabiyyan” is an adjective describing the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: نعت للقرآن. وجوز أبو البقاء أن يكون

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ allows “ʿArabiyyan” as a circumstantial accusative from “Qurʾānan,” if that word is understood to contain a pronoun and to denote a derived state: sent down assembled in Arabic.
rows.anchor: وجوز أبو البقاء أن يكون حالا من الضمير في

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Arabic” is ascribed to the Arabs because the revelation came in their language; the singular nisba is ʿArabī, parallel to Rūmī for one Roman.
rows.anchor: والعربي منسوب للعرب لأنه نزل بلغتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAraba, with fatḥa on rāʾ, is a district associated with the dwelling of the prophet Ishmael.
rows.anchor: وعربة بفتح الراء ناحية دار إسماعيل النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s line witnesses the place-name ʿAraba; its rāʾ is quiesced for poetic necessity, so “Arabic” could also be ascribed to that locality.
rows.anchor: وعربة أرض ما يحل حرامها من الناس إلا اللوذعي الحلاحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “qaṣaṣ” means the recounted content, “aḥsan” is an object: the best things recounted, with the verbal noun used like a passive noun or a passive-form word.
rows.anchor: منصوبا على المفعول به، ولكن إذا جعلت القصص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “qaṣaṣ” remains an active verbal noun, “aḥsan” is an explanatory cognate-object accusative and the object meaning “what is recounted” is omitted: the best recounting.
rows.anchor: والثاني: أن يكون منصوبا على المصدر المبين، إذا جعلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Aḥsan” may be a true comparative or simply mean “good”; on the latter reading the genitive construction is an adjective annexed to its described noun.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن تكون أفعل تفضيل على بابها، وأن تكون لمجرد الوصف بالحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ in “bi-mā” marks cause, attaches to “We recount,” and “mā” is a verbal noun: because of Our revelation.
rows.anchor: الباء سببية، وهي متعلقة ب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent parsing makes “this Qurʾān” the direct object of “We revealed.”
rows.anchor: وهو الظاهر أن ينتصب على المفعول به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second parsing treats “this Qurʾān” as disputed between “We recount” and “We revealed,” with the later verb governing it; this works only if “aḥsan” is a cognate-object accusative and no omitted object is supplied for “We recount.”
rows.anchor: أن تكون المسألة من باب التنازع، أعني بين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording “though before it you were among the unaware” has a parallel discussed earlier.
rows.anchor: قوله: " وإن كنت " إلى آخره تقدمه نظيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The strongest analysis makes “idh” a past-time adverb governed by Jacob’s “he said, O my son” in the next verse, locating Yusuf’s dream report at that time.
rows.anchor: في العامل فيه أوجه، أظهرها: أنه منصوب ب

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makkī makes “idh” governed by “among the unaware.”
rows.anchor: الناصب له " الغافلين " قاله مكي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making “idh” governed by “We recount” takes it out of its ordinary past-time adverbial sense; even supplying “the situation at the time” still requires that shift.
rows.anchor: وهذا فيه إخراج " إذ " عن المضي وعن الظرفية، وإن قدرت المفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another option supplies an unexpressed command, “remember.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو منصوب بمضمر، أي: اذكر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats “idh” as an encompassing apposition to “the best narrative,” since the time contains the story.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو منصوب على أنه بدل من " أحسن القصص " بدل اشتمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads the tāʾ of “yā abati” with fatḥa; the other readers use kasra. The tāʾ replaces the first-person yāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر بفتح التاء، والباقون بكسرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This replacement-tāʾ occurs only in “yā abati” and “yā ummati,” not in other nouns; “yā ibn umm” belongs to a related special rule.
rows.anchor: وهذا يختص بلفظتين. يا أبت، ويا أمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry permits combining the tāʾ with a yāʾ or alif despite the ordinary prohibition; he gives three poetic examples.
rows.anchor: ويجوز الجمع بين هذه التاء وبين كل من الياء والألف ضرورة كقوله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the kasra preceding the possessive yāʾ shifts onto the tāʾ because feminine tāʾ requires a preceding fatḥa; the tāʾ, as a full consonant, must remain vocalized.
rows.anchor: فزحلقت إلى التاء لاقتضاء تاء التأنيث أن يكون ما قبلها مفتوحا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī argues that tāʾ replaces the yāʾ alone, not its preceding kasra, so retaining the kasra does not combine a substitute with what it replaces; “yā abatā” likewise combines tāʾ with an alif replacing yāʾ.
rows.anchor: التاء عوض من أحد الشيئين وهو الياء، والكسرة غير متعرض لها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the kasra’s survival as in “yā ghulām”: it signals annexation and remains meaningful beside the substitute tāʾ.
rows.anchor: بل حالها مع التاء كحالها مع الياء

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The shaykh likewise says tāʾ replaces the possessive yāʾ, cannot join it, but may join the substitute alif, citing “yā abatā.”
rows.anchor: وهذه التاء عوض من ياء الإضافة فلا تجتمعان، وتجامع الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Samīn objects that alif itself replaces yāʾ, so joining it to the tāʾ should also count as combining substitute and replaced element.
rows.anchor: وفيه نظر من حيث إن الألف كالياء لكونها بدلا منها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the ending is feminine tāʾ used instead of the possessive yāʾ, citing its change to hāʾ in pause as evidence.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت: ما هذه التاء؟ قلت: تاء تأنيث وقعت عوضا من ياء الإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀmir pause on hāʾ, while the other readers retain tāʾ, treating it like the tāʾ in “bint” and “ukht”; Sibawayh reports al-Khalīl’s analysis of it as feminine tāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ به ابن كثير وابن عامر، والباقون وقفوا عليها بالتاء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī defends feminine tāʾ on a masculine vocative by comparison with gender-marked words that can describe males; al-Samīn says it feminizes only the word’s form.
rows.anchor: قلت: يعني أنها جيء بها لمجرد تأنيث اللفظ كما في الألفاظ

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says feminine marking can replace possessive marking because both are suffixes attached to the end of a noun; al-Samīn rejects this as a superficial formal analogy.
rows.anchor: لأن التأنيث والإضافة يتناسبان في أن كل واحد منهما زيادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reports “yā abati” with three case vowels; al-Samīn accepts the attributed fatḥa and kasra but calls the ḍamma reading very unusual and compares it with a vocative annexed to yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وأما الضم فغريب جدا، وهو يشبه من يبني المنادى المضاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kasra has two explanations: al-Zamakhsharī says the pre-yāʾ kasra shifted to tāʾ; another view adds an independent kasra to signal the replaced yāʾ. Al-Samīn regards the disagreement as minor.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم توجيه كسر هذه التاء بما ذكره الزمخشري

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Fārisī’s first account treats fatḥa as standing for the alif that derives from yāʾ, as in “yā ibn umm” and “yā ibn ʿamm”; an anonymous verse supplies a parallel.
rows.anchor: أنه اجتزأ بالفتحة عن الألف، يعني عن الألف المنقلبة عن الياء

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Fārisī’s second account deletes tāʾ in a vocative shortening, then inserts an open tāʾ; al-Samīn compares the construction with al-Nābigha’s line addressed to Umayma.
rows.anchor: أنه رخم بحذف التاء، ثم أقحمت التاء مفتوحة، وهذا كما قال النابغة

rows.speaker: الفراء وأبو عبيد وأبو حاتم وقطرب
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ, Abū ʿUbayd, Abū Ḥātim, and Qutrub’s first view treats the alif of “yā abatā” as a lamenting-vocative ending later omitted in favor of fatḥa; some reject it because this is not lament.
rows.anchor: أن الألف في " با أبتا " للندبة، ثم حذفها مجتزئا عنها بالفتحة

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub’s other account derives the form from “yā abatun,” with tanwīn dropped because vocatives often omit it; the objection is that tanwīn remains in an accusative vocative such as “yā ḍāriban rajulan.”
rows.anchor: أن الأصل: يا أبة بالتنوين، فحذف التنوين لأن النداء باب حذف

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar reads “yā abī,” retaining the yāʾ and using no replacement tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر " يا أبي " بالياء، ولم يعوض منها التاء

rows.speaker: الحسن وطلحة بن سليمان
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Ṭalḥa ibn Sulaymān read “aḥada ʿashar” with a quiescent ʿayn, apparently marking the two words as one compound name.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وطلحة بن سليمان: " أحد عشر " بسكون العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the wāw coordinates, the sun and moon may be singled out after the eleven stars because they are included among them, as Gabriel and Michael are named after the angels; alternatively, they may be additional objects seen.
rows.anchor: لأن الشمس والقمر دخلا في قوله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī transmits both interpretations: the sun and moon are either included among the eleven stars or are additional to them.
rows.anchor: والاحتمالان منقولان عن أهل التفسير، وممن نقلهما الزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wāw may mean “with,” making the sun and moon additional to the eleven stars, but this is weaker because ordinary coordination works without awkwardness or loss of meaning.
rows.anchor: والوجه الثاني: أن تكون الواو بمعنى مع، إلا أنه مرجوح

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The shaykh regards “I saw them prostrating to me” as a repeated clause for emphasis after the long intervening objects, like the repeated clause in the cited verse.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أنها جملة كررت للتوكيد لما طال الفصل بالمفاعيل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says it is a new answer to an implied question from Jacob about how Yusuf saw the stars, sun, and moon; al-Samīn finds this stronger than emphasis because it adds new information.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت: ما معنى تكرار " رأيتهم "؟ قلت: ليس بتكرار، إنما هو كلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Sājidīn” uses the rational masculine plural because the celestial bodies are treated as rational when their action is attributed to them, by analogy from a shared property.
rows.anchor: لأنه لما عاملهم معاملة العقلاء في إسناد فعلهم إليهم جمعهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vision is a dream; dream-seeing, like cognitive seeing, takes two objects, so the second object after “I saw eleven stars” is omitted only by ellipsis, since omission for restriction is impossible and ellipsis is rare or rejected by some.
rows.anchor: والرؤية هنا منامية، وقد تقدم أنها تنصب مفعولين كالعلمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading keeps both ṣāds distinct, the Hijaz dialect; Zayd ibn ʿAlī assimilates them into one doubled ṣād, the Tamīm dialect.
rows.anchor: قرأ العامة بفك الصادين وهي لغة الحجاز. وقرأ زيد بن علي بصاد واحدة مشددة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats “ruʾyā” as “seeing” restricted to sleep, distinguished from waking vision by the feminine-ending pattern, as with “qurba” and “qurbā.”
rows.anchor: الرؤيا بمعنى الرؤية، إلا أنها مختصة بما كان في النوم دون اليقظة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ruʾyā” is a verbal noun, like “buqyā.”
rows.anchor: والرؤيا مصدر كالبقيا. وقال الزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has hamza without imāla; al-Kisāʾī, in al-Dūrī’s transmission, gives imāla here. Both “ruʾyā” forms in this sūra are imālated by al-Kisāʾī, while Abū ʿAmr changes the hamza to wāw through al-Sūsī.
rows.anchor: وقرأ العامة " الرؤيا " بهمز من غير إمالة، وقرأها الكسائي في رواية الدوري عنه بالإمالة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reports assimilated forms “riyāk” with either ḍamma or kasra on rāʾ but calls them weak, since the underlying wāw stands for hamza and does not assimilate strongly, like the hamza in “ittazara” and “ittajara.”
rows.anchor: وسمع الكسائي " رياك " و " رياك " بالإدغام وضم الراء وكسرها، وهي ضعيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra in “riyāk” avoids a yāʾ in sukūn after ḍamma; with ḍamma, the yāʾ is treated as consumed by assimilation.
rows.anchor: وأما كسر " رياك " فلئلا يؤدي إلى ياء ساكنة بعد ضمة، وأما الضم فهو الأصل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: “Fa-yakīdū” is subjunctive as the result of the prohibition, understood as condition and consequence; al-Zamakhsharī paraphrases: if you tell them, they will plot against you.
rows.anchor: منصوب في جواب النهي وهو في تقدير شرط وجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Kaydan” is most naturally an emphatic cognate accusative.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: وهو الظاهر أنه مصدر مؤكد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains “laka” by saying “yakīd” is made to carry a verb that takes lām, expressing both plotting and scheming for added force, reinforced by the cognate accusative.
rows.anchor: ضمن معنى فعل يتعدى باللام ليفيد معنى فعل الكيد

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The shaykh treats lām as an alternative transitive marker, like verbs such as “naṣaḥa” and “shakara”; al-Samīn objects that this is a restricted, nonproductive pattern and “kāda” is not listed.
rows.anchor: كذا قاله الشيخ وفيه نظر، لأن ذاك باب لا ينقاس

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ calls the lām an extra direct-object marker, as in the cited “radifa lakum”; al-Samīn rejects this because extra lām requires an advanced complement or a derived verb.
rows.anchor: اللام زائدة في المفعول به كزيادتها في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis makes the lām causal, “for your sake,” with the object omitted, either by restriction or ellipsis.
rows.anchor: الرابع: أن تكون اللام للعلة، أي: فيكيدوا من أجلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fifth analysis makes “laka” a circumstantial phrase modifying “kaydan,” originally an adjective delayed from it.
rows.anchor: الخامس: أن تتعلق بمحذوف، لأنها حال من: " كيدا " إذ هي في الأصل

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: If “kaydan” is a direct object meaning a plot they devise against you, it is a verbal noun functioning as a substantive, as in “assemble your plot.”
rows.anchor: أي: ما تكيدون به، ذكره أبو البقاء وليس بالبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With “kaydan” as a direct object, only the lām-as-adjective-now-circumstantial or causal analyses remain; the other three lām analyses do not apply.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا ففي اللام في " لك " وجهان فقط: كونها صفة في الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāf in “wa-kadhālika” may be accusative as a circumstantial complement of an understood verbal noun, an analysis attributed to Sībawayh, or as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun: “like that great choosing.”
rows.anchor: فالنصب: إما على الحال من ضمير المصدر المقدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively the kāf is nominative, the predicate of an omitted subject: “the matter is thus.”
rows.anchor: والرفع على خبر ابتداء مضمر أي: الأمر كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Wa-yuʿallimuka” begins a new clause outside the comparison, with an understood subject: “and He will teach you.”
rows.anchor: قوله: { ويعلمك } مستأنف ليس داخلا في حيز التشبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some treat “aḥādīth” as an irregular broken plural of the attested singular “ḥadīth,” alongside other unusual plural patterns.
rows.anchor: الأحاديث: جمع تكسير، فقيل: لواحد ملفوظ به وهو " حديث " ولكنه شذ جمعه على أحاديث

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abū Zayd posits an unattested singular “uḥdūtha”; al-Samīn rejects classifying “aḥādīth” as a collective because this pattern is specific to broken plurals, especially where no singular is attested.
rows.anchor: وزعم أبو زيد أن لها واحدا مقدرا وهو أحدوثة ونحوه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls “aḥādīth” a collective noun for “ḥadīth,” not a plural of “uḥdūtha”; al-Samīn says the latter point matches the majority, though al-Zamakhsharī may not mean “collective noun” literally.
rows.anchor: ولهذا رد على الزمخشري قوله: " وهي اسم جمع للحديث وليس بجمع أحدوثة "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “ʿAlayka” may attach either to “yutimma” or to “niʿmatahu.”
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يتعلق ب " يتم " ، وأن يتعلق ب " نعمته "

rows.speaker: البصريون
rows.claim: The Basran rule repeats “ʿalā” before “the family of Jacob” so coordination can attach to the genitive pronoun.
rows.anchor: وكرر " على " في قوله: " وعلى آل " ليمكن العطف على الضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Min qablu” means “before you.”
rows.anchor: وقوله: " من قبل " أي من قبلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ibrāhīm wa-Isḥāq” may be an appositive to “your two fathers,” an explanatory apposition, or an explicit “I mean” construction.
rows.anchor: قوله: { إبراهيم وإسحاق } يجوز أن يكون بدلا من " أبويك " أو عطف بيان

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads singular “āya,” intended generically; the other readers use the plural to make explicit that there were many signs.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير " آية " بالإفراد، والمراد بها الجنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed omitted phrase “and for others besides those asking” is unnecessary.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن ثم معطوفا محذوفا تقديره: للسائلين ولغيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Li-s-sāʾilīn” modifies “āyāt” as an adjective through an omitted element.
rows.anchor: و " للسائلين " متعلق بمحذوف نعتا لآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Aḥabb” is a comparative built from passive-form “ḥubb,” an irregular derivation; with love or hate, “ilā” marks the experiencer, while lām or “fī” marks the one loved or hated.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { أحب إلى أبينا }: " أحب " أفعل تفضيل، وهو مبني من " حب " المبني للمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays’s line uses “aḥabbu ilaynā,” confirming that the father is the experiencer who loves Yusuf more.
rows.anchor: قال امرؤ القيس: 2740 لعمري لسعد حيث حلت دياره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām before Yusuf is the emphatic lām of initiation; “aḥabb” is the predicate of the coordinated pair and does not match in gender or number under the comparative rule.
rows.anchor: واللام في " ليوسف " لام الابتداء أفادت توكيدا لمضمون الجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wāw in “wa-naḥnu ʿuṣbatun” introduces a circumstantial clause, and the common reading has “ʿuṣbatun” as its nominative predicate.
rows.anchor: والواو في " ونحن عصبة " للحال، فالجملة بعدها في محل نصب

rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين
rows.claim: A reading attributed to the Commander of the Faithful puts “ʿuṣbatan” in the accusative, with an omitted predicate such as “we see” or “we gather,” leaving “a group” as a rare circumstantial substitute.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أمير المؤمنين بنصبها على أن الخبر محذوف، والتقدير: نحن نرى

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī compares the omitted predicate to the Arabic expression “innamā al-ʿāmirī ʿammatuhu”; the shaykh objects that “ʿuṣba” is neither verbal noun nor manner noun, while al-Samīn says the intended analogy is simply deletion with another element filling the gap.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: " هذا كما تقول العرب: " إنما العامري

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad analyzes “ḥukmuka musammaṭan” as “your judgment is yours, sent forth and not rejected,” citing al-Farazdaq; another estimate inserts “thabata.” Al-Samīn objects that “musammaṭan” could itself be the predicate, so the example is anomalous under the stated rule.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: " هو من باب " حكمك مسمطا "

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās defines “ʿuṣba” as more than ten, and also as ten to forty.
rows.anchor: ما زاد على عشرة، عن ابن عباس، وعنه: ما بين عشرة إلى أربعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other definitions make “ʿuṣba” three people; a group from above three through nine is “raht,” and ten or more is “ʿuṣba.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: الثلاثة نفر، فإذا زاد على ذلك إلى تسعة فهم رهط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Further definitions range from one to ten, ten to fifteen, six, or seven people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ما بين الواحد إلى العشرة. وقيل من عشرة إلى خمسة عشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root conveys surrounding or encircling, as a headband encircles the head.
rows.anchor: والمادة تدل على الإحاطة من العصابة لإحاطتها بالرأس

rows.speaker: الحوفي وابن عطية
rows.claim: Al-Ḥawfī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya take “arḍan” as if a preposition “fī” were omitted, as in the cited Qurʾānic phrase and an anonymous verse.
rows.anchor: أن تكون منصوبة على إسقاط الخافض تخفيفا أي: في أرض

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads “arḍan” as an adverbial accusative because it is indefinite and vague: an unknown, distant, uninhabited land.
rows.anchor: أرضا منكورة مجهولة بعيدة من العمران، وهو معنى تنكيرها

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects the adverbial analysis: the land is qualified as remote, and Yusuf must already be on some land, so the brothers mean a different distant land from his father’s vicinity.
rows.anchor: وذلك خطأ؛ لأن الظرف ينبغي أن يكون مبهما، وهذه ليست كذلك

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The shaykh approves Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s objection: “I sat a distant house/place” needs “fī,” whose omission is limited to poetic necessity or the disputed verb “dakhala.”
rows.anchor: وهذا الرد صحيح لو قلت: جلست دارا بعيدة أو مكانا بعيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Samīn objects that a vague adverbial is what has no enclosing boundaries; “arḍan” in this verse fits that category.
rows.anchor: إذ الظرف المبهم عبارة عما ليس له حدود تحصره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third analysis makes “arḍan” a second object if “throw him” entails “send him down,” which takes two objects, as in the cited verse.
rows.anchor: الثالث: أنها مفعول ثان، وذلك إن تضمن " اطرحوه " أنزلوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ṭarḥ” means throwing and can figuratively mean plunging oneself into dangers; ʿUrwa ibn al-Ward’s line illustrates the metaphor.
rows.anchor: والطرح: الرمي، ويعبر به عن الاقتحام في المخاوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Yakhlu” is the result clause of the command, with either assimilation or clear articulation, discussed earlier at the cited verse.
rows.anchor: جواب الأمر، وفيه الإدغام والإظهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ reads “ghiyābāt” in both occurrences of the sūra, treating the place as parts each called a concealed recess; most readers have singular “ghiyābat.”
rows.anchor: جعل ذلك المكان أجزاء، وسمي كل جزء غيابة

rows.speaker: ابن هرمز
rows.claim: Ibn Hurmuz agrees with Nāfiʿ’s plural but doubles the yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وابن هرمز. كنافع إلا أنه شدد الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The strongest derivation of Ibn Hurmuz’s reading is an intensive active-participle form, originally descriptive.
rows.anchor: والأظهر في هذه القراءة أن يكون سمي باسم الفاعل الذي للمبالغة

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Fārisī classifies the form with nouns on “faʿāl,” such as Sibawayh’s “fiyād”; Ibn Jinnī cites “fakhār,” meaning pottery.
rows.anchor: وألحقه الفارسي بالاسم الجائي على فعال نحو ما ذكر سيبويه

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: The author of al-Lawāmiḥ allows either “faʿalāt,” like “ḥammāmāt,” or “fayʿalāt,” like “shayṭānāt,” both intensive plural patterns.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون على فعالات كحمامات، ويجوز أن يكون على فيعالات

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads “ghaybah” with fatḥa on yāʾ, which may be a verbal noun like “ghalabah” or a plural of “ghāʾib,” like “ṣāniʿ/ṣanaʿa.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن: " غيبة " بفتح الياء، وفيها احتمالان، أحدهما

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The shaykh reports a form in Ubayy’s codex with quiescent yāʾ, meaning the darkness of the well; al-Samīn questions how such a vowel can be known from an unvocalized codex.
rows.anchor: قال الشيخ: " وفي حرف أبي " غيبة " بسكون الياء، وهي ظلمة الركية "

rows.speaker: الهروي
rows.claim: Al-Harawī defines a “ghiyāba” as a recess or ledge above the water in a well that hides what is inside from view.
rows.anchor: شبه لجف أو طاق في البئر فويق الماء يغيب ما فيه عن العيون

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī places the concealed recess at the bottom of the well: its base is broad and its mouth narrow, so a viewer cannot see into its sides.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: " الغيابة تكون في قعر الجب؛ لأن أسفله واسع

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī defines it as the well’s depth, hidden from the observer and dark below; al-Munkhil’s line uses “ghiyābatī” for a grave.
rows.anchor: هي غوره وما غاب منه عن عين الناظر وأظلم من أسفله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Jubb” may name a well because it is dug into rough ground or cut into earth; it has the plurals “jubbaba,” “jibāb,” and “ajbāb.”
rows.anchor: والجب: البئر التي لم تطو، وتسميته بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has masculine agreement in “yaltaqiṭuhu”; al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Abū Rajāʾ, and Qatāda use feminine agreement, by semantic femininity and feminine annexation, as in “some of her fingers.”
rows.anchor: قرأ العامة " يلتقطه " بالياء من تحت وهو الأصل. وقرأ الحسن ومجاهد وأبو رجاء وقتادة بالتاء من فوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of “if you are doing” is omitted: doing what will accomplish your aim.
rows.anchor: ومفعول " فاعلين " محذوف أي: فاعلين ما يحصل غرضكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Sayyāra” is the plural of “sayyār,” an intensive pattern.
rows.anchor: والسيارة، جمع " سيار " ، وهو مثال مبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Iltqāṭ” is taking up something cast aside, the same root as “luqṭa” and “laqīṭ”; an anonymous line witnesses the usage “iltqāṭan.”
rows.anchor: والالتقاط: تناول الشيء المطروح، ومنه: " اللقطة " واللقيط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Lā taʾmannā” is circumstantial; a similar analysis was given earlier.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { لا تأمنا }: حال وتقدم نظيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading’s “ikhfāʾ” weakens the vowel and separates the two nūns; the first is not fully quiescent, which would make the reading assimilation rather than concealment.
rows.anchor: قرأ العامة " تأمنا " بالإخفاء، وهو عبارة عن تضعيف الصوت بالحركة

rows.speaker: الداني
rows.claim: Al-Dānī says most of his authorities use this ikhfaʾ, which is correct because its articulation is clear and its analogy sound.
rows.anchor: قال الداني: " وهو قول عامة أئمتنا وهو الصواب لتأكيد دلالته وصحته في القياس "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read with ishmām: lip-rounding signals the verb’s vowel while the nūns are fully assimilated; the difficult gesture may be made during or after assimilation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعضهم ذلك بالإشمام، وهو عبارة عن ضم الشفتين إشارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One use of ishmām mixes a kasra with some ḍamma, as in “qīla” and “ghīḍ”; another mixes one consonant into another, as ṣād is colored toward zāy in “al-ṣirāṭ” and “wa-man aṣdaq.”
rows.anchor: ومنها إشراب الكسرة شيئا من الضم نحو:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another use signals ḍamma only in pause and is visible to the sighted but not the blind.
rows.anchor: ومنها الإشارة إلى الضمة في الوقف خاصة، وإنما يراه البصير دون الأعمى

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر والحسن
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar reads with complete assimilation and no ishmām; al-Ḥasan reads with clear articulation to emphasize the verb’s inflectional vowel.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر بالإدغام الصريح من غير إشمام. وقرأ الحسن ذلك بالإظهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority agree on either ikhfaʾ or ishmām, as described.
rows.anchor: اتفق الجمهور على الإخفاء أو الإشمام كما تقدم تحقيقه

rows.speaker: ابن هرمز
rows.claim: Ibn Hurmuz reads “taʾmannā” with ḍamma on mīm, transferring the first nūn’s vowel when it is to be assimilated after mīm loses its vowel; the one-nūn spelling of the codex conflicts with al-Ḥasan’s reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن هرمز " لا تأمنا " بضم الميم، نقل حركة النون الأولى

rows.speaker: أبو رزين وابن وثاب
rows.claim: Abū Razīn and Ibn Waththāb read with kasra on the imperfect prefix; Ibn Waththāb also eases the hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو رزين وابن وثاب " لا تيمنا " بكسر حرف المضارعة

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The shaykh says context after “mā laka” signals a negation, not a prohibition, and that assimilation could confuse it with negation.
rows.anchor: قال الشيخ: " ومجيئه بعد " مالك " والمعنى يرشد إلى أنه نفي لا نهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Samīn says confusion with a prohibition is remote, though the shaykh is right that assimilation could cause confusion with negation.
rows.anchor: قلت: وما أبعد هذا عن توهم النهي حتى ينص عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Samīn lists fourteen readings: six among the seven canonical readings and eight irregular ones, varying subject, vowel and deletion of weak yāʾ, case ending, and active or passive voice.
rows.anchor: فهذه أربع عشرة قراءة، منها ست في السبع المتواتر وثمان في الشاذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ reads “yartaʿu wa-yalʿabu” with yāʾ and kasra on ʿayn.
rows.anchor: قراءة نافع بالياء من تحت وكسر العين. الثانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Bazzī from Ibn Kathīr reads “nartaʿu wa-nalʿabu” with nūn and kasra.
rows.anchor: قراءة البزي عن ابن كثير " نرتع ونلعب " بالنون وكسر العين

rows.speaker: قنبل
rows.claim: Qunbul has two readings, with or without final yāʾ both in pause and continuation; one matches al-Bazzī’s reading.
rows.anchor: الثالثة: قراءة قنبل، وقد اختلف عليه فنقل عنه ثبوت الياء بعد العين

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن عامر
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read with nūn and sukūn on both verb endings.
rows.anchor: قراءة أبي عمرو وابن عامر " نرتع ونلعب " بالنون وسكون العين والباء

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: The Kūfans use yāʾ with sukūn on both endings.
rows.anchor: قراءة الكوفيين: " يرتع ويلعب " بالياء من تحت وسكون العين والباء

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad reads “nartaʿ” with nūn and “yalʿab” with yāʾ; the same is transmitted from Ibn Kathīr.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جعفر بن محمد " نرتع " بالنون " ويلعب " بالياء

rows.speaker: العلاء بن سيابة
rows.claim: Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Siyāba reads both verbs with yāʾ, kasra on ʿayn, and ḍamma on bāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ العلاء بن سيابة " يرتع ويلعب " بالياء فيهما وكسر العين

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة وابن محيصن
rows.claim: Mujāhid, Qatāda, and Ibn Muḥayṣin read the first verb with nūn bearing ḍamma and both endings quiescent.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد وقتادة وابن محيصن " نرتع " بضم النون وسكون العين والباء

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء
rows.claim: Abū Rajāʾ has the same quiescent endings, but uses yāʾ for both verbs.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو رجاء كذلك، إلا أنه بالياء من تحت فيهما

rows.speaker: النخعي ويعقوب
rows.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī and Yaʿqūb read “nartaʿ” with nūn and “yalʿab” with yāʾ.
rows.anchor: والنخعي ويعقوب " نرتع " بالنون و " يلعب " بالياء

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads both verbs with yāʾ in the passive.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي " يرتع ويلعب " بالياء من تحت مبنيين للمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading retains yāʾ in “nartaʿi” and raises “nalʿabu.”
rows.anchor: وقرىء " نرتعي ونلعب " بثبوت الياء ورفع الباء

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads “narʿā wa-nalʿabu.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي عبلة " نرعي ونلعب "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn readings make Yusuf’s brothers the subjects; yāʾ readings make Yusuf the subject. Kasra on ʿayn treats the form as a jussive with deleted weak letter from “iftaʿala” of grazing.
rows.anchor: فمن قرأ بالنون أسند الفعل إلى إخوة يوسف، ومن قرأ بالياء أسند الفعل إليه دونهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn on ʿayn treats the verb as jussive by deleting its vowel, deriving it from “ratiʿa-yartaʿ” for luxuriating in abundant pasture; an anonymous line illustrates “ratiʿ.”
rows.anchor: ومن سكن العين اعتقد أنه جزمه بحذف الحركة وجعله مأخوذا من رتع يرتع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn on bāʾ makes “yalʿab” jussive, while its ḍamma marks an independent clause, “and he plays.”
rows.anchor: ومن سكن الباء جعله مجزوما، ومن رفعها جعله مرفوعا على الاستئناف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading with yāʾ on “yalʿab” but nūn on “nartaʿ” suits the children’s play to the young Yusuf.
rows.anchor: ومن غاير بين الفعلين فقرأ بالياء من تحت في " يلعب " دون " نرتع "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The quadriliteral “nartaʿ” has an omitted object: “we pasture our livestock.”
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ: " نرتع " رباعيا جعل مفعوله محذوفا، أي: نرعي مواشينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the passive, the suppressed object is understood as “tomorrow”: originally the verbs take “fīhi,” then the preposition is omitted, the pronoun becomes an object, and when passivized it becomes the raised subject pronoun.
rows.anchor: المفعول الذي لم يسم فاعله وهو ضمير الغد، والأصل
